title: 2 Kings 13:1–13
context: Jehoahaz son of Jehu reigns over Israel, and the LORD gives Israel into the hands of Hazael and Benhadad of Syria for following the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. When Jehoahaz pleads, the LORD gives Israel a savior, yet the people keep their idolatry and the Asherah remains in Samaria (the WEB prints verses 5–6 as a parenthesis). His son Jehoash (also called Joash) continues in the same sins. The synchronisms between the kings of Israel and Judah are not simple to reconcile, and proposed reckonings vary. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about covenant discipline, God’s mercy, and persistent sin.

verses.text: In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria for seventeen years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoahaz son of Jehu begins a seventeen-year reign over Israel in Samaria, dated by Joash of Judah’s reign. The regnal formula sets the frame.

Arminian readers see a new king given a real opportunity to lead Israel back to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
The synchronisms between Israel’s and Judah’s kings in these chapters are not simple to harmonize, and interpreters propose various reckonings.

Reformed readers see God ruling over the succession of kings. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold chronological reconstructions tentatively.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin. He didn’t depart from it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoahaz does evil in the LORD’s sight and follows the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. He does not depart from them.

Arminian readers see a king who, like his predecessors, freely chooses the worship Jeroboam devised over obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ‘sins of Jeroboam’ recall the calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28–30). The refrain recurs throughout Kings.

Reformed readers see the persistent grip of entrenched idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the king’s responsibility for Israel’s worship.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger burned against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael, continually.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s anger burns against Israel, and he gives them into the hands of Hazael and Benhadad of Syria. Judgment comes through a foreign power.

Arminian readers see covenant discipline responding to Israel’s continued unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hazael’s rise had been foretold to Elisha’s grief (2 Kings 8:12). The oppression is presented as the LORD’s doing.

Reformed readers see God directing nations to discipline his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground; how God uses hostile agents is treated at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Jehoahaz begged the LORD, and the LORD listened to him; for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoahaz begs the LORD, and the LORD listens, because he sees Israel’s oppression. Even an evil king’s plea is heard.

Arminian readers see prayer genuinely moving God to respond with mercy (compare the box at Joshua 10:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
The text grounds God’s hearing in his seeing the people’s suffering, echoing Exodus language of God seeing oppression.

Reformed readers see prayer as a means God uses to bring about his merciful purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s compassion.

verses.text: (The LORD gave Israel a savior, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians; and the children of Israel lived in their tents as before.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD gives Israel a savior, and they escape Syria’s hand and live in their tents as before. The WEB prints verses 5–6 as a parenthesis.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious answer to the cry of verse 4.
verses.reformedNotes:
The savior is not named. Proposals include Jehoash, Jeroboam II, or outside pressure on Syria, but the text does not say.

Reformed readers see deliverance as God’s gift. Both traditions read this as shared ground and leave the deliverer’s identity open.

verses.text: Nevertheless they didn’t depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, with which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.)
verses.arminianNotes:
Even so, Israel does not depart from the sins of Jeroboam’s house, and the Asherah remains in Samaria. Deliverance does not produce reform.

Arminian readers see mercy received without the repentance it invited.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parenthesis closes on a sober note. Relief from oppression and renewed faithfulness are not the same thing.

Reformed readers see the persistence of idolatry even under kindness. Both traditions read this as shared ground about receiving God’s help without turning to him wholeheartedly.

verses.text: For he didn’t leave to Jehoahaz of the people any more than fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen; for the king of Syria destroyed them and made them like the dust in threshing.
verses.arminianNotes:
Syria has left Jehoahaz only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen, made like dust at threshing. Israel’s army is shattered.

Arminian readers see the cost of Israel’s unfaithfulness laid out plainly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse resumes the account after the parenthesis, explaining how weak Israel had become.

Reformed readers see human strength reduced so that any rescue would plainly be God’s. Both traditions read this as shared ground and draw no further conclusions than the text gives.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Jehoahaz’s acts and his might are referred to the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The narrator is selective.

Arminian readers see Kings focusing on covenant faithfulness rather than a full political record.
verses.reformedNotes:
The cited chronicle is not the canonical book of Chronicles; it appears to be a source no longer extant.

Reformed readers see Scripture recording what serves its theological purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the selective nature of the history.

verses.text: Jehoahaz slept with his fathers; and they buried him in Samaria; and Joash his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoahaz dies and is buried in Samaria, and his son Joash reigns in his place. The dynasty of Jehu continues.

Arminian readers see the passing of a king whose prayer was heard but whose reign brought no reform.
verses.reformedNotes:
The dynasty’s continuation fits the promise given to Jehu of four generations on the throne (2 Kings 10:30).

Reformed readers see God keeping his word to Jehu’s house. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his stated word.

verses.text: In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria for sixteen years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash son of Jehoahaz begins a sixteen-year reign in Samaria in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah. The names Joash and Jehoash are both used.

Arminian readers see another generation given its own opportunity to return to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
The synchronism here and in verse 1 has prompted proposals of overlapping reigns or differing reckoning systems; none is certain.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over each reign. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep chronological reconstructions hedged.

verses.text: He did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight. He didn’t depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin; but he walked in them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoash also does evil and walks in all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. The pattern continues.

Arminian readers see a king who freely persists in the inherited idolatry rather than breaking with it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verdict repeats almost word for word the judgment on his father in verse 2.

Reformed readers see the hardening power of settled national sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting that the repetition underlines the north’s unbroken path away from the LORD.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, and his might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Joash’s acts, including his war against Amaziah of Judah, are referred to Israel’s chronicles. That war is narrated in chapter 14.

Arminian readers see the narrator pointing ahead to events still to be told.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary mentions Amaziah before the story of their conflict appears, a feature of the narrative arrangement.

Reformed readers see the narrator shaping the history for its message. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground about the structure of Kings.

verses.text: Joash slept with his fathers; and Jeroboam sat on his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joash dies, is buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and Jeroboam sits on his throne. His closing formula comes before the Elisha story.

Arminian readers see the narrator turning from royal records to the prophet’s final word.
verses.reformedNotes:
This Jeroboam is the son of Joash, often called Jeroboam II, whose reign appears in 14:23–29. The regnal close is repeated at 14:15–16.

Reformed readers see the arrangement highlighting the prophetic word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the narrative’s structure.
